title: Why white audiences accept him and black audiences make him work
summary: Black audiences must warm up while whites accept him at once; he explains the mixed repertoire that gets him hired.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Was there a conscious transition to playing for all white audiences?
No, I don't think... Not for me. Because what I can remember is being an entertainer, the first thing you look for is who will accept you as you. The white audience accepted me as me. That was it.
You have to work hard for them. And that's even today.
How do you mean work hard?
In other words, you got to be at your maximum best at every setting. See, so what I'm saying is this. You come in and the blacks first have to wait until they get half drunk.
It's getting back to that saying.

Yes, to accept you. Whereas white, they hired me from me from the beginning. Blacks did the same thing. But they got to wait until they get drunk to get into it. Whites accept from the beginning. Boom.
Did you feel you were appreciated more by whites?

I'll tell you what. And you just ask. Start with the Neville brothers, Irma Thomas, Gene Knight, Oliver. And just ask them. They're going to tell you the same thing I'm saying. Hey, man, look. If there was a way. Well, I could. You know. Now, playing these social clubs is a different thing because you get set into playing a certain way. Okay. You know that people are going to come in there and sit down. You know the other people are going to sit down until they get half juice. And then they'll let loose. And we know that the Creoles are going to start letting loose just like white people write off. So, you know, this is understanding. And me being a band leader, these are the things that I know. So I know how to give my band to the audience. And see, one of the reasons why I get hired, too, is because they say that, Bartome, you know how to play for us. And what they mean is that I'll play a mix, a mixture of music. I play some old, some new, standards. I play cha-cha if you didn't have to. And stardust. And things like that. Whereas a lot of the young bands would come in and they'd get to playing that loud, blabber, blabber music right off. And it don't fit the situation. Don't know how to play a waltz. You see what it is? Now, I know how to play a ball. I haven't played but one strict ball. And that was for St. Mary's Academy. See, when I say a strict ball, they have a king and queen. And everything is done in St. Mary's. You know, like a ball. Okay. Well, the blacks' balls are just a bit different. They have the king and the queen. But it's a little more loose. And I know how to play it. I got it copped off and they hired me for this specific reason. You know? No, no. And that's how I keep working.
